doc.title: Dave Liebman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Jerry Coker, Aebersold and deciding to teach
summary: He recalls Coker's ear and Aebersold's clinics, and concludes teaching would give him a living and meaning.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Coker knew everything backwards and forwards and could hear a pin drop and play it back to you.
With two hearing aids, which is all the more amazing.

He would do the scale syllabus. Friday, you had to do the scale syllabus. Played all the scales in any key, Jamey playing in front of all the kids, 10 o’clock. With me, he’d tell me. He’d say, B-flat Dorian, okay, do whatever. Jerry would do it by ear. Jerry would just start playing. He’d just do it by ear. That’s how bad he was, amazing. And Jamey, being Jamey, just his whole personality, the [?] and the books, the whole thing. I didn’t know. So now, by ’80, ’81, I’m starting to see this teaching thing a little bit and also realizing that – because my career’s not at the greatest point now. I’m definitely in a dip – how am I going to make a living? This jazz thing is not going to pay, ever. I’m not a star. It’s not going to pay. I do not want to do studio work. I am not doing club dates any more. I want to do something for the world, and I need to make a living. Teaching. That was it. That was the decision that I made.
